vignette:
It feels so different now. Before, she used to thrive on the chaos—the adrenaline of the siren, the weight of the gear, the shared, wordless rhythm of the crew pulling hoses through smoke. At forty-one, Lena has been a firefighter for sixteen years, and she earned her place through sheer grit. She would say she had a body built for it, a mind that could lock onto a task and not flinch. She still wears the uniform, still shows up for every shift, but the person inside it has changed.

Two years ago, she was diagnosed with a rare, aggressive form of lung cancer. The doctors linked it to decades of inhaling toxic smoke, the kind that settles deep and doesn’t wash out. At the time, she had no symptoms except a persistent cough she blamed on the job. The biopsy came back like a sledgehammer. Within a week, she was on a surgical table with a thoracic surgeon removing a lobe of her right lung. Then came twelve rounds of chemotherapy, each one leaving her hollowed out, her muscles wasting, her hair falling out in clumps. She remembers lying in a hospital bed, staring at the ceiling tiles, thinking, *This is how I die. Not in a fire. In a bed. Quietly.*

She survived. But the survival has not felt like a victory. It feels like a thin, fragile membrane stretched over a deeper terror that never stopped.

In the present, Lena’s days are governed by intrusion. The thoughts arrive without warning—usually at night, when the station is quiet and she lies on her bunk, listening to the hum of the diesel engine. The memory of the diagnosis, the exact words of the oncologist, the cold echo of the CT scanner, all of it plays back in high definition. Sometimes the flashback is visceral: she feels the chemical burn of the IV, tastes the metallic nausea. She has learned to press the heels of her palms against her eyes until she sees stars, trying to scramble the images.

At work, she has become cautious to the point of paralysis. In a structure fire, her heart slams against her ribs not from exertion, but from a raw, animal dread that has replaced her old courage. She volunteers for the less risky tasks—driving the truck, managing the hose from outside—avoiding the interior search that once defined her. Her captain has noticed. He pulled her aside last week and asked gently if she was okay. She said she was fine. She is not fine. She avoids medical checkups, even the routine physicals the department requires. The thought of a blood test or an X-ray sends her into a cold sweat, her legs trembling, and she has called in sick twice just to escape the appointment.

Her husband, Mark, tries to understand. He holds her at night when she startles awake, gasping for air, certain she cannot breathe—though her oxygen saturation is perfect. She has convinced herself that every chest twinge is the cancer returning. She checks her body in the mirror obsessively, prodding her ribs, searching for lumps she knows are not there. She has stopped planning for the future. When Mark talks about vacation next summer, she changes the subject. She cannot imagine herself alive that far ahead.

The guilt is crushing. She used to be the one the crew relied on for calm—the paramedic who could talk a jumper off a ledge, the firefighter who would crawl into a collapse without a second thought. Now she feels like a fraud. She believes she is weak, broken, unworthy of her badge. She has started to pull away from her closest friends in the station, afraid they will see the fear in her eyes.

She still goes to work. She still puts on the gear. But the part of her that used to love the job, that used to feel invincible, is gone. In its place is someone who lives every day waiting for the next diagnosis, the next verdict, the next quiet end.
